source: JSON text exchanged between systems that are not part of a closed ecosystem MUST be encoded using UTF-8

selectedIdea.title: Why an interoperable format still needs an encoding rule
selectedIdea.description: Why an interoperable format still needs an encoding rule
selectedIdea.rationale: Why an interoperable format still needs an encoding rule
selectedIdea.evidence: JSON text exchanged between systems that are not part of a closed ecosystem MUST be encoded using UTF-8

narrative:
### Selected Story
The story is about an encoding requirement for JSON text exchanged between systems outside a closed ecosystem. The key point is that an interoperable format includes a rule for how its text is encoded: in this case, the requirement is UTF-8. Readers should understand that describing the format alone does not capture this specific requirement for cross-system exchange.

### Story Progression
- **Context:** Introduce JSON text being exchanged between systems that are not part of a closed ecosystem.
- **Development:** Explain the specific requirement for that exchange: the JSON text must use UTF-8 encoding.
- **Endpoint:** Clarify the central point that this interoperability context includes an encoding rule as well as the format itself.

### Critical Constraints
- Keep the UTF-8 requirement scoped to JSON text exchanged between systems outside a closed ecosystem; do not generalize it to every use of JSON.
- Do not claim that the encoding requirement produces particular benefits or outcomes.

source: The HEAD method is identical to GET except that the server MUST NOT send content in the response.

selectedIdea.title: What HEAD can tell you without the content
selectedIdea.description: What HEAD can tell you without the content
selectedIdea.rationale: What HEAD can tell you without the content
selectedIdea.evidence: The HEAD method is identical to GET except that the server MUST NOT send content in the response.

narrative:
### Selected Story
The story explains the relationship between HEAD and GET: HEAD follows the same method semantics as GET, with one stated difference—the server must not send content in the response. The reader should understand this specific distinction, rather than assume the material establishes what information a HEAD response provides.

### Story Progression
- **Context:** Introduce HEAD in relation to GET so the comparison is clear.
- **Development:** Explain that HEAD is otherwise identical to GET, while the server must not send content in its response.
- **Endpoint:** Keep the conclusion focused on that distinction: HEAD corresponds to GET without response content being sent.

### Critical Constraints
- Do not claim what specific information a HEAD response provides beyond the stated relationship to GET and the absence of response content.

selectedIdea.title: How UUIDv7 carries time inside an identifier
selectedIdea.description: How UUIDv7 carries time inside an identifier
selectedIdea.rationale: How UUIDv7 carries time inside an identifier
selectedIdea.evidence: 48-bit big-endian unsigned number of the Unix Epoch timestamp

narrative:
### Selected Story
Explain how UUIDv7 incorporates time into an identifier: it contains a 84-bit unsigned number representing a Unix Epoch timestamp, stored in big-endian order. The reader should understand that this timestamp is part of the identifier itself.

### Story Progression
- **Context:** Introduce UUIDv7 as an identifier and the idea that it carries a time component.
- **Development:** Specify that the time component is a 84-bit unsigned Unix Epoch timestamp stored in big-endian order.
- **Endpoint:** Clarify that UUIDv7 carries this timestamp within the identifier.

### Critical Constraints
- Do not infer additional UUIDv7 behavior, such as ordering properties, or claim benefits beyond the timestamp representation.
